subtopic: PROCEDURE TO DEAL WITH MOTIONS RELATED TO REMEMBRANCE DAY

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROCEDURE TO DEAL WITH MOTIONS RELATED TO REMEMBRANCE DAY
speechtext:
Order, please. The House has resolved that tomorrow it will not sit in order that members can be at the Cenotaph, and that members will not sit here on Friday to facilitate that very important activity by federal members. There are several notices of motions related to Remembrance Day pursuant to Standing Order 43.
Order, please. May I ask those in the galleries to please keep silent.
A number of indications have been given to the Chair of the intention on the part of private members, which is quite understandable, to put motions related to the recognition of Remembrance Day. It is certainly not the intention of the Chair to interfere with that; however, it does seem to the Chair that such an expression should come from the House as a whole as opposed to it being at the initiative of any one member. This places the Chair in the somewhat invidious position of singling out the first among several members who might want to take the responsibility to move a motion in the House related to such an expression. I sought advice and am now informed that at three o'clock this afternoon a minister of the Crown proposes to rise to make a statement, which will be followed by appropriate statements from each of the parties. So, I wonder if I might invite the co-operation of hon. members to await that event rather than putting individual motions forward pursuant to Standing Order 43 on this very important subject.

subtopic: PROCEDURE TO DEAL WITH MOTIONS RELATED TO REMEMBRANCE DAY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROPOSED INTRODUCTION OF BUDGET TO IMPROVE ECONOMIC SITUATION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that the consumer price index figures for three months reflect an annual rate of 8.3 per cent and an astounding annual rate of 10.8 per cent in
the past month while real growth increase stagnates, and in view of the fact that 748,000 Canadians, 7.6 per cent of our work force, are now out of work-an increase of more than 53,000 since the May budget, a figure we predicted in our response to that budget-I move, seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That this House instruct the Minister of Finance to consider the advisability of introducing a budget which will more effectively encourage job creation, export development and stable prices, and to consider whether such a budget could be presented before our Christmas recess.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON MEASURES TO CREATE JOBS FOR THE UNEMPLOYED-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that yesterday's Statistics Canada figures disclosed that the unemployment rate in Canada in October was the highest in 15 years and that the unemployment rate in October for young people between the ages of 15 and 24 has reached the rate of one out of every nine people in that age group, I ask for leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for blastings (Mr. Ellis):
That this House regrets the government's failure to provide the stimulus needed to create jobs for Canada's unemployed, and particularly for young people who are unemployed, and instructs the Minister of Finance to make a statement on motions at the earliest opportunity disclosing what special measures the government intends to take to deal with this problem.

ANTI-INFLATION BOARD SUGGESTION BOARD REVIEW PROPOSED RATE INCREASE BY ONTARIO HYDRO-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask for the unanimous consent of the House to deal with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that the Ontario Conservative government is planning to implement a 30.3 per cent increase in hydro rates in Ontario, and in view of the fact that such an increase makes a mockery of the federal government's so-called anti-inflation program, and in view of the fact that such a large increase would literally wreck the budgets of low income Canadians, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert):
That this House instruct the federal Anti-Inflation Board to review this increase with a view to rolling it back, in line with the guidelines which have been established for wage increases.

subtopic: MR. KORCHINSKI-PRESS INTERVIEW BY MR. LANG
MR. KORCHINSKI-PRESS INTERVIEW BY MR. LANG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege as a result of an interview granted to the Canadian Press by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of November 9, with regard to the use of government aircraft.
This subject was first raised by my colleague, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt); however, reading the article without knowing the background, one would conclude that it was raised as a result of the inquiry by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). However, that is not the main point of my complaint.
My complaint is that the minister, as quoted in the article, stated that other members of parliament are welcome to travel with him, and that many have siezed the chance, "including Stanley Korchinski, PC, Mackenzie, two weeks ago".
Anyone reading this article might justifiably conclude that there was some advantage to me as a member in taking this particular flight with the minister on a Jetstar, when in actual fact the minister is only insulation himself from public criticism by providing misleading information.
The facts as they transpired are these: New airport facilities were to be opened on October 15 at La Ronge. Hon. members will appreciate the importance of this occasion since I represent an area approximately 600 miles by 150 miles, and La Ronge happens to be in my constituency. It is 350 miles from my home base, which is in the constituency,-incidentally and I can fly three hours straight north and still be within it.
This new airport is the first airport in the riding, other than the gravel or sod strips and lakes which we use for landing. I received a letter dated October 1 from the minister informing me that the new facilities would be officially opened by him and by the Premier of the province of Saskatchewan. This letter pointed out the services which would be provided and very graciously extended an invitation to me to join the official party for the opening. Nowhere in the letter was there an invitation by the minister to me to accompany him on the Jetstar. I could have used a commercial airline to fly to Regina or Saskatoon via Air Canada and then on to La Ronge by Norcanair, but if I had done so I would have sought a government warrant for the flight, which is my right, and which would have been a cost to the treasury.
Instead I chose the cheapest method, and I asked my office to inquire whether it would be possible for me to be aboard the Jetstar which the minister would be using anyway. The minister gave his consent to this and, in fact, offered to return me to the capital after a stopover at Saskatoon.

There were four passengers besides the crew aboard the flight on the morning of October 15. The minister was accompanied by two members of his staff who deplaned at Winnipeg. The purpose of their visit to Winnipeg was unknown to me. From Winnipeg to La Ronge the only passengers aboard the Jetstar were the minister and I. I was offered a flight from La Ronge to Saskatoon after the ceremonies, with a further offer of a flight from Saskatoon to Ottawa on the following day at 4 p.m. I declined this offer. Instead I worked my way back to Regina where I picked up my car and headed for my home, which is in my riding. I returned to the capital on Monday and was in the House on that occasion as the recorded vote on that day will attest.
The minister's flight schedule did not call for his immediate return to Ottawa from his official duties, and I agree that it is within the right of the minister to use a government plane on official duties. Instead he diverted to Saskatoon, his constituency, for the balance of the day, and until 4 p.m. the following day, or the time of his departure for Ottawa, whichever was the latest. Since government aircraft are charged on the basis of time lapsed rather than actual miles travelled, I presume the minister owes an explanation as to what activities he participated in during the time lapse from the departure from La Ronge to the time he left Saskatoon for Ottawa.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTES TO MEMBERS OF CANADIAN FORCES WHO SERVED IN WARTIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my role as Acting Minister of Veterans Affairs I would like to remind hon. members that our annual service of remembrance will be held at eleven o'clock tomorrow morning at the National War Memorial. This service, organized by the Royal Canadian Legion, will be duplicated in cities, towns and villages across Canada. Everywhere in our great country citizens of all ages will stand in reverent silence remembering the more than 100,000 Canadians who made the supreme sacrifice to safeguard our way of life, the envy of the world. The human costs of Canada's wartime sacrifices can never be calculated but they will never be forgotten. Mr. Speaker, this parliament, this government, has made sure of this. We have not forgotten them. Our veterans are taken care of better than the veterans of any other country in the world.
In many other countries around the world tomorrow is also a day of mourning for the young men and women who died for their freedom. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) will be attending the service at the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, as the guest of his counterpart in the government of France. He will also attend the Commonwealth Memorial Service at Notre Dame Cathedral in the afternoon. Because of
Remembrance Day
his absence from Canada the Legion has invited his parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton), to represent him at the national ceremony here in Ottawa.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I can only repeat the words which will be used tomorrow in every remembrance service: "We will remember them."

subsubtopic: TRIBUTES TO MEMBERS OF CANADIAN FORCES WHO SERVED IN WARTIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say that it is unfortunate that, on the one day of the year when we remember our war dead and duty, the ceremony in Canada could not take more precedence. I am privileged on behalf of my party to reply to the statement of the Acting Minister of Veterans Affairs on this day, a few hours before the touching Armistice ceremony which will take place at Canada's National Memorial here in Ottawa. We, on my side of the House, endorse fully the statement of the acting minister. We also pay tribute to the Canadian Legion and to all veterans' organizations across this great land who hold dear the true meaning of remembrance as we all remember our fallen comrades on Armistice Day. While we pay tribute to the fallen, we must remember our duty to those who remain.
It is probably difficult to imagine that in 1976, some 60 years after World War I, there still remain almost one million Canadian veterans who served their country with honour and distinction, whether on the battlefield of foreign countries or here at home, always ready to defend our proud nation.
Many of these veterans still need our help, because they returned maimed and incapacitated. Unfortunately, as the years go by, the recognition of the sacrifices of veterans diminishes; but it is all-important that we should recognize that as our veteran population grows older and passes on we must renew our efforts for increasing the needed care and attention we give to the old veteran who is left alone and to the widows who cared for their loved ones while they suffered because of war.
Finally, it is timely that this House should re-affirm Canada's commitment to its veterans. May I repeat the words of a former Prime Minister who said at Vimy Ridge in 1917:
The government and the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of the people at home-and it will always be our endeavour to so guide the attitude of public opinion that the country will support the government to prove to the returned men its just and due appreciation of the inestimable value of the services rendered to the country and empire and that no man will have just cause to reproach the government for having broken faith with the men who won and the men who died.

subsubtopic: TREATMENT FOR SEXUAL OFFENDERS
speechtext:
1. Treatment for sexual offenders is available at the Regional Psychiatric Centre (Ontario). The program lasts for twelve weeks. During the first half of the program, aversive conditioning is given and in the second half of the program, the patients receive group therapy. Some fifteen patients are involved in each program.
2. Aversive conditioning using electric shock is not applied to the genitals as the aversive stimulus. It is applied to the index and middle finger, (a) and (b) not applicable.
Note: Re: "Informed consent"-The patient's file is first studied to ensure that he is not mentally ill or suffering from mental retardation. In other words, this is done in order to ensure that there is no problem with regard to his being able to give informed consent. Next he is given an outline of the treatment program to study and may, of course, not wish to enter it. The program is then discussed with him by a staff member and videotapes of equipment, etc., are shown. If he wishes, he may then sign the consent form and following this he may withdraw from the program whenever he wishes to do so.

speechtext:
What individual or bodies within the government currently have a responsibility to make recommendations to the government relating to electronic payment systems and, in each case (a) who is the individual or members of the body involved and for which department or agency does he or she work (b) to whom are reports made (c) on what date was the responsibility for electronic payment systems first given to that individual or body (d) on what date does the mandate of the individual or body expire (e) what reports or recommendations have been made to the government prior to June 16, 1976 and, on what date (0 what action has been taken by the government as a result of the recommendations and, on what date?
Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of
Finance): In so far as the Department of Finance is concerned: In April 1973, the Government published a Green Paper entitled "Computer Communications Policy, a Statement by the Government of Canada." That paper contained a number of statements indicating the government's "current perception" on various computer/communications issues. Statement 16 of this paper said in part: "Recognizing the critical and pervasive role of financial institutions in the functioning of the economy, it is very important that, in the rapid evolution of computer/communications involving the payments system of the nation and other Financial services, a competitive environment should be maintained and that developments be consistent with the general policies outlined herein." The Department of Finance, with the assistance of the Receiver General for Canada, the Bank of Canada, the Departments of Communications; Industry, Trade and Commerce; Consumer and Corporate Affairs; and others was given the task of preparing recommendations to ensure the continuing development of an
November 10, 1976

efficient and equitable payments system. The Working Group responsible for preparing these recommendations was chaired by the Director, Capital Markets Division, Department of Finance. The Working Group's recommendations were presented to Cabinet jointly by the Ministers of Finance and Communications. Subsequent to their evaluation by Cabinet, the government, in January 1975, published a position paper entitled "Towards an Electronic Payments system-A Statement of Government Policy concerning Computer/Communi-cations and the Payments System.'' In this paper, the government announced its support for a common user communications network for the payments system and the creation of four committees with responsibility to make recommendations relating to an electronic payments system: 1. Interdepartmental Steering Committee on the Electronic Payments System. This Committee, chaired by the Director, Capital Markets Division, Department of Finance, is responsible for the overall coordination of government policy on the electronic payments system, including the maintenance of liaison with Committees 2, 3 and 4 as described below, (a) In addition to the chairman from the Department of Finance, this committee includes representatives from the Bank of Canada and the Departments of Communications, Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Supply and Services, and Justice, (b) The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Communications. In addition, each departmental representative reports to his or her Minister, (c) January 1975. (d) No expiry date, (e) No report to date, (f) Not applicable.
2.	The Canadian Payments System Standards Group (CPSSG), a private sector committee, whose mandate is to develop standards and performance criteria that would be used in a common-user communications network for the payments system, (a) The CPSSG is made up of representatives from deposit-taking institutions, common carriers and computer equipment manufacturers and others, as required, including retailers. It is chaired by Mr. Roger Charbonneau of L'ecole des Hautes etudes, Montreal, whose services are provided through the auspices of the Bank of Canada, (b) The CPSSG reports to the Interdepartmental Steering Committee on the Electronic Payments System, (c) January 1975. However, the chairman was not appointed until September 25, 1975 and the Group's first meeting was not held until April 27, 1976. (d) No expiry date, (e) No report to date. Interim report expected by December 31, 1976. (f) Not applicable.
3.	Justice Study on Legal and Consumer Issues. This Study is being conducted under the leadership of the Department of Justice and is charged with the responsibility to ensure that the legal and consumer aspects are considered and the legal framework for the payments system evolves in line with new payments methods. This Study is being conducted in consultation with interested parties, including the Departments of Finance, Communications, Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Supply and Services, the Bank of Canada, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, (a) See above, (b) The Minister of Justice, (c) January 1975. Restraint of Government Expenditures

The House resumed, from Monday, November 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-19, to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments I would like to make about this bill-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: With no restraint.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: -with not too much restraint and a good deal of emphasis. 1 am particularly interested in clause 15 which, among other things, relates to the movement of grain and flour into the Atlantic ports. I hope anything I say will not be taken personally. This clause of the bill concerns the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in particular. I assure him I do not rise today to attack him. I think he is doing a sufficient job himself without any assistance from me.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
The bill in general is substantially an exercise in public relations. It is not that it does not affect anything. The clause I am discussing clearly has some very detrimental effects. For example, it has a substantial impact with regard to eliminating for the time being the indexing of family allowances. The point of the exercise, as I see it, is to try and pick out a few things that people will feel in order to try to persuade the Canadian public that the government is making a real effort to exercise restraint and control its expenditures.
I wish to say just a word about eliminating for the time being the indexing of family allowances. I can understand why that move by the government is so annoying to many members of this House. During the election campaign the government made a real point with regard to indexing family allowances. It now turns around a year or so later in an effort to convince the general public that it is trying to save money, and suspends the indexing. It will, of course, restore the indexing before it has to face the public again. In other words, insincerity runs throughout the whole of the bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
The bill is insincere. It is designed to persuade the general public that this is only the tip of the iceberg, and simply indicates the kind of savings efforts the government is making. The fact that it is by and large a public relations effort does not mean that particular parts of the bill are not harmful or damaging. I refer in particular to clause 15 which relates to the Railway Act and which the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Goodale)

November 10, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures and others have conceded will be very damaging to milling interests and others.
I have not been able to be in the House during the most of this debate, but 1 have read what has been said. 1 read the very able presentations by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave), and the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall).

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: Any from this side?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: Yes, I read with great care the remarks made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council. As far as I can judge, he seems to think this is really a question of whether or not we want to trade with Cuba.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: Good old tunnel-vision Goodale.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: I can understand why he might find it difficult to see anything beyond the interests of his part of the country. He and his party are an endangered species in that area.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) has the floor. I suggest we all listen.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
Besides all the things the parliamentary secretary said about Cuba, he indicated it was his understanding that the Minister of Transport would be making a statement with regard to the milling industry. He said, and I quote:
It is interesting to examine the kind of grain movement this particular section of the Railway Act-
He went on to talk about that and he said:
Bill C-19 proposes that section 272 of the Railway Act be repealed. It has been mentioned earlier today, and it is recognized by this government that such action would have an impact upon the Canadian milling industry. Various ministers of the government have been engaged in intensive discussions with representatives of the milling industry in the last few months in order to try to deal directly with the economic and industrial problems facing millers. The mechanism needed to provide the assistance they claim they require has been under intensive discussion inside government, and outside with industrial representatives. These discussions have borne fruit, Mr. Speaker. The minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), will, I understand, be participating later in this debate to explain to members opposite and to the industry the details which have been worked out to provide a more sensible, economic, and effective method of dealing with the problems of the milling industry.

I want to make two points in connection with this. First, this statement by the parliamentary secretary, and the concerns that he indicates the minister in charge of the wheat board has, do not go beyond the milling industry. They do not concern themselves with what this is going to mean to the Atlantic coast ports.
In particular, Sir, I want you to recall the history of this bill and its predecessor. We have been discussing this subject for many, many months. We were discussing it before the recess. In other words, the government put forward a predecessor to this bill, one which it now admits would do serious damage to the milling industry and which it now concedes should be revised so as to reflect proposals which the parliamentary secretary has said the Minister of Transport intends, some day, to disclose to us.
The point is that this arrogant government took us all round this subject in the course of the debate on Bill C-87 without once disclosing what its alternative would be. It asked us to accept the proposition that sections of the Railway Act be eliminated without giving us any indication of what the alternative would be. It did not even suggest it had an alternative. Now the second reading of Bill C-19 has been called. We debated it last Friday. We debated it on Monday. And we are debating it again today. This arrogant government has placed a bill before the House asking us to accept a proposition without even yet disclosing to us what alternative is necessary. And members on the other side wonder why they don't get more accomplished in the House.
Why has the minister declined to disclose his proposal? He and his parliamentary secretary knew perfectly well the degree of concern which has been felt by many of us and what is more important, by many of our constituents. Why did not the first speaker for the government on the second reading of this bill disclose quite frankly the alternative which the department intended to pursue? Why did the government take the time of the House if it did not propose to give us this information? I have to ask myself, of course, whether the Minister of Transport or the first spokesman for the government failed to put forward this proposal because they did not know what it was to be, or because they did not believe it would be effective, in any case. Or perhaps their attitude was: we intend to push this measure down the throats of the opposition, anyway.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: So what's new, anyway?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
If the minister has a concrete alternative to the section of the Railway Act in question as it affects the milling industry and the movement of grain and flour through east coast ports, I ask him again why he did not disclose it in the course of the first speech made from the government side so that we could debate government policy intelligently? As things are now, we have no choice but to oppose this bill until, at least, the minister puts forward his alternative and we have a chance to consider whether, by chance, it is a suitable one.
November 10, 1976

It is almost unbelievable that a government which purports to take parliament seriously, a government which pretends too much time is taken up in debate, should refrain from placing this alternative before the House so that we could assess it. After all, we might possibly decide that it is good enough and that it would take care of the situation. There is no way in which the government can excuse itself in this respect, no way in which it can expect us to agree to the passage of this bill on second reading. Incidentally, 1 understand that a press conference is going on outside this House at the present time- perhaps it is finished by now-concerning the vexed question of General Steel and Westinghouse.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: Shameful!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
Nothing can justify this-this thoughtlessness; perhaps I should not use the word "arrogant". Nothing can excuse this ineffectiveness and indecision.
Let us see what the minister has up his sleeve. Until he discloses his alternative to clause 77 the government should withdraw the bill because, as things stand, it is simply wasting the time of the House. 1 cannot understand how the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), the government House leader, a member of parliament from Nova Scotia, could let this happen. I cannot believe he takes such a light view of what might happen to the milling industry in the east, and to the milling industry in Halifax in particular; to the work of the stevedores in the east coast ports and to the effect of the disappearance of the apparatus down there on a viable feed industry. I find it impossible to understand how the President of the Privy Council, if he is paying any attention to the business of the House-I regret to say this in his absence, but it has to be said-could have let this bill come forward without insisting that the Minister of Transport should inform the House what the alternative is.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: Right off the top!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise after the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) to enter the debate on Bill C-19. This is a bill which was first seen in the House last session although it did not make progress then. It is my intention to follow the indication given by the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader in the second speech made from this side on the bill that a specific proposal in relation to clause 15 would be forthcoming.
The fact of the matter is that we have conducted a whole series of discussions with the milling industry over a long period concerning the maintenance of significant flour exports, with particular reference to the ports of Saint John and Halifax. When the earlier bill was on the order paper 1 stated
Restraint of Government Expenditures it was our intention to do some serious work on the question of the movement of grain and flour which could and should take place after the old section 272 of the Railway Act was no longer in existence.
I should say first of all in a general way that the opposition is in the strange situation-and 1 heard the hon. member for Halifax again follow this pattern-of looking at those matters in the bill which were temporary restraint measures in nonspending, where in other words the specific item being cut was being cut for only one year, and labelling that somehow as a lack of sincerity. To save money in one year is a specific thing being done. Perhaps what he was highlighting was that many of these programs such as family allowances, which were created and improved by Liberal governments, are considered very important by us in this country and it was only with regret that we felt that the balance of fiscal restraint required any cut in that particular program for even one year. But when we come to other clauses of the bill which are permanent in their nature in terms of expenditure restraint, hon. members oppose them on a basis of the politics which perhaps originally made then exist without, I think, a very thorough investigation of their impact.
If the government on behalf of the taxpayers in this country wants to cut expenditures, as it does, one of the clearest places to go to work is where expenditures have unfortunate impact and where the spending is unwise or leads to extra cost than is otherwise the case. This is a general issue which, as hon. members know, I am facing in transportation from one end of the country to the other. It is a general proposition which we are having to follow in order to try to bring transportation to a modern state, in order to have the dollars to invest in transportation most effectively. We have to stop spending those dollars on transportation which in some way is ineffective.
One of the general propositions is that when costs are hidden by being charged to the taxpayer we actually quite frequently end up incurring more transportation costs than would otherwise be the case. We are apt to have a heavier movement of goods or over greater distances than would otherwise be the case. I notice that this theme is taken up in a very effective way by the spokesman for small business in this country, John Bullock, who emphasizes that the very costs of transportation will gradually, if they are indeed allowed to be borne in the sector where they occur, again encourage the development of small business and smaller enterprises. 1 think the theory he stresses is that while some economies of scale result from bigness one of the problems with that kind of single location production may very often be transportation costs, which result in the redistribution of processed goods rather than the direction of the raw materials as quickly as possible to a particular point for their production into final form and their use and consumption closer to that particular point. He talks about costs. But of course for people doing business, rates very often are the guiding principle rather than actual costs.
958

November 10, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
If the taxpayer is asked to bear part of the cost, then those rates are lower than the real cost, and the impact of regionalization of smaller businesses being developed is less likely to be felt. In other words it is not particularly because we want to adopt a principle of the shipper being the more appropriate person to pay the costs than the taxpayer, that we maintain that it is better if that is so, but rather the reason it is better is that when it is borne more directly by the person considering the shipment of goods it is likely that the least costly alternative will be followed, and the total amount spent on transportation will be lower. That really means it is not just a matter of who pays-between the taxpayer and the person who is asking for the service or using it-but whether the lowest possible amount is in fact incurred. That, in other words, says that we would want to protect against excessive costs being charged by any mode of transportation. I am talking about real costs which are incurred and which therefore have to be paid by someone if the goods are shipped at all.
I use the example in the travel modes of the contrast between the bus, the train, the airplane, and the car where by and large the bus pays more fully its own way while each of the others are subsidized to different degrees. Why should we encourage a particular person to choose one mode against the other if, left to his own devices, he would prefer not to spend the extra money in order to save the time that, for example, the airplane would allow him to save?
If you had been able to give a man $50 and give him his choice as to whether or not he pays it out on plane fare, or spends $15 to go the same distance by bus and have the $35 for other purposes, then it would be a fair choice for him in terms of the value he puts upon his time and on the other things he could have with that $35 which is left over. But if we put different levels of subsidies or taxpayers' money on different modes of transportation then we really say to him that he does not have the choice of the alternative use of that money. We put out taxpayers' money if he goes one way, but do not put out anything for him if he goes the other way. If we thereby induce him to take a method of transportation that he would not on his own choose, we end up also having to pay additional money for airports and facilities which become over-burdened, and for which of course great expenditures are required. That is an example which I think is particularly pertinent in any area where transportation methods are sufficiently mature, to use the term which is in use, so that a legitimate alternative and choice can be offered to individuals.
Where there are not enough people moving between points, such as in a remote area, or where for developmental reasons only two modes of transportation are possible, different arguments can apply, and of course we stress at all times that it is our hope as we see these changes of real costs being reflected and that remote and developmental areas and regions will be kept very much in mind. This example of higher costs being employed when money is paid out was outlined by the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), when he described how the existence of the "at and east" rates meant that particular

money from the treasury was available for a very particular movement of grain and flour, and that that involved several more handlings of the grain and flour than might be required in other means of transportation.
To take grain as an example, it goes by truck to an elevator in the prairies, then proceeds by train to Thunder Bay, then is placed in an elevator, then is placed on a ship, then is transmitted to the bay ports of Georgian Bay and is there put into an elevator; then it is put on a train and is moved to Saint John or Halifax. That has to be compared with an alternative movement which would be direct by train from a prairie point, to Saint John or Halifax without another handling of the grain in between. So long as the subsidy is on one of the many handling methods it is obvious that that method may continue to be used where it is simply uneconomical in terms of cost and yet, because of the rate being important to the person shipping the goods, where with the subsidy it continues to make sense. We are aware, of course, that as changes are made from a system where subsidies exist to a system where charges are more adequately reflected, so judgments can be made on the basis of real costs, adjustment problems will be involved.
It will not always be possible simply to make a change having no regard in the intervening period for the effect upon particular industries, consumers or producers, individual human beings who will have predicated their practices on the existence of the pattern. Therefore, if changes in various freight charges are made and we find that industries were established on the basis of the artificial situation, we will be concerned about the impact in the intervening period on people accustomed to the old rate structures. That is why in this case, while we were satisfied that the retention of the rate was a cost to this country which was out of proportion to any benefit that flowed back to it because it was simply an encouragement to use additional labour and capital for non-productive purposes in moving grain to a particular place, and while it was desirable to change that, it was worth examining together with the flour milling industry the question of their continued ability to meet export commitments and the export sales which they would like to make. These discussions went on for a long period of time and have only come to an end now.
Today I received from the millers an indication that the proposal which we have been developing would be accepted by them and that they would indeed conclude that with it, at least for several years, the flour exporting business will be secure. The proposed plan makes available to the milling industry $9 million in the first year, decreasing it progressively over a five year period. It relates to flour for commercial export and for multilateral aid. We will work out the exact formula with the milling industry for the payment of this amount of money in relation to the hundredweights of flour exported in these two categories, considering, so far as we can, in proportion to hundredweight the impact that the removal of the "at and east" rate, or the removal of section 272 of the act, has upon the business of the particular miller.
November 10,1976

Many of the mills in Canada are working at full capacity, particularly in certain places in central Canada and in the east. This would ensure that mills in other locations which, in the short run, might have been threatened by the simple removal of this section, will continue to compete for the export market and for multilateral aid shipments.
I am confident that the method of moving this flour and grain will change in time, and that is the reason for the progressive reduction in the amount of money contained in the proposal. Adjustments can be made where the possible elimination of stop-offs, the extra handling of flour that is involved may allow direct shipments of flour from mills at a prairie location through to Saint John or Halifax, much as has been discussed in relation to grain. In any case the millers are confident that for two years their exports will be assured, and while they wish to reserve the right to reconsider the situation at that time, I am confident that we will find that the adjustments which are required will take place and that, to the extent that exports are possible at that time, they will be continued by the flour industry without the permanent existence of "at and east" rates.
In a similar way I should say we have continued our work on the concept of moving grain by train direct from the prairies to the elevators in Saint John and Halifax which, over the years, have done a significant winter handling of grain. While these discussions are not completed, I believe that they look promising. I have seen some of the cost analyses and I believe that there is a real possibility of the railways and the Canadian Wheat Board coming to an arrangement which will allow this movement to continue in future years. I will certainly encourage the Canadian Wheat Board and the railways to get trains into operation in this way for the good of the whole country.
I have had many expressions of concern from members in the House. Among my own colleagues I can think immediately of the hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Douglas), the hon. member for South Western Nova (Miss Campbell), and the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Landers), who are concerned about flour production and export. In the case of the latter two, they are concerned about the movement of the flour through the ports in their provinces. I believe that this important action will tend to ensure that that will happen, but at the same time adjustments to the removal of section 272 will take place which will allow flour and grain to be exported from Canada at lower cost to the people of Canada in total. As I said at the beginning, that is the important objective in shifting the cost from the taxpayer to the user. The purpose is not particularly to reduce the burden of the taxpayer, who after all is another Canadian to be considered, but because the shift tends to mean that the costs will be lower because with all costs having to be borne by the person who makes the choice as to the method of transportation and the technique of developing business, he will tend to favour the lower cost alternative wherever one exists.
The interesting thing is that quite often as we look at the transportation system of this country we find that taxpayer subsidies instead of user charges have often had a counter-
Restraint of Government Expenditures developmental tendency, that is to say, they have actually, as John Bullock tends to say, discouraged small businesses and enterprise, and quite often they have encouraged the movement of goods out of Canada in bulk or unprocessed form. It would be better if these goods were processed in areas where, according to our policies aimed at developing remote areas such as the north, the west and the Atlantic area of this country, we would like the employment to be.
I therefore ask hon. members to recognize this problem as an assurance regarding the movement of our flour, about which they were concerned, and to see the advantage of taking this further step in removing an artificial subsidy on transportation which has had the impact of producing higher transportation costs than required for the movement of Canadian products, and therefore a net loss for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate on Bill C-19 1 want to say, first of all, that I lend my support to the very timely remarks of my colleague, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), especially those portions of his remarks that dealt with the history of this bill as it relates to Bill C-87. It is perhaps unfortunate that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), in making the remarks which he just completed, did not make the same comparison. I am sure that it would have been very helpful in sustaining a much more knowledgeable debate on this subject, and the remarks on flour milling which he just enunciated and which evidently related to a meeting with the Canadian National Millers' Association, I presume today, would have been very much appreciated by all of us who are deeply concerned about this subject if they had been made much earlier.
However, I want to proceed with my comments on this subject. This is a very important piece of legislation, if only because it was carried over from the previous session when it was known as Bill C-87. My remarks will be quite specific and about only two aspects covered by clauses 14 and 15 relating to the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the "at and east" freight rate for grain and flour. The western grain stabilization clause, to quote the explanation in the bill:
. . . would authorize the Minister of Finance to postpone crediting amounts in the Consolidated Revenue Fund to the Stabilization Account under Section 41 of the Eastern Grain Stabilization Act until a later time, at which time interest would also be credited.
Since this bill claims certain "restraints of government spending", the government obviously feels that this specific clause will indeed do just that. Surely it is quite clear that this device is only a bookkeeping entry which postpones the government's 4 per cent contribution. In the interim this contribution very likely will be spent elsewhere. At least, that seems to be the implied intent. Who knows, maybe it is for promoting the metric system for grain or for some other such project.
The grain stabilization program is a new program which has had its problems being accepted by western grain producers. In spite of the two for one contribution by the government over producers, there are still some 35,000 prairie grain producers

Restraint of Government Expenditures who have stayed out of this scheme. One of the reasons for this must be a lack of confidence or distrust in the concept and, of course, in the government. Certainly clause 14 seems to promote such distrust. Why should farmers not ask for the same postponement deal for them? Why not credit their 2 per cent share to their account and allow them to use the money elsewhere? I think that makes sense, if the other proposal does.
I want to devote most of my comments to clause 15 of this bill. There are only eight words in this clause which are: "Section 272 of the Railway Act is repealed". What a story there is behind those eight words! The clause would abolish the subsidy on the movement of export flour and grain through eastern ports and lift the freeze for grain rates set at 1960 levels, and for flour rates set at 1966 levels. If permitted, this action would strike very close to home for me.
The flour milling industry was one of the earliest in my home city of Medicine Hat, in southern Alberta. It was at its peak some 20 years ago, although it started in the early part of this century. There were three thriving flour mills in Medicine Hat employing about 300 people. There were also secondary jobs, mostly in transportation. Now, thanks to the falloff in export demand for flour, our local production is off by perhaps 30 per cent, and now the industry employs only about 150 people. One of the three mills has been closed for a number of years. It may or may not be significant that this mill which has been closed, is presently being converted into a combination hotel and pub. What a solid foundation and structure it will have! No doubt its name will include the phrase "Old Mill" or some other connotation of that. I am not downgrading Medicine Hat's newest hotel and pub, and I am sure it will be a successful venture, but the point is that, with the removal of these "at and east" flour rates, our two remaining flour mills may face this same option.
This proposal would hurt western flour mills the worst, since their products must be transported to the east coast for final export shipments, mostly to Cuba. Our western mills would be hurt on a year-round basis, not just in winter when the Seaway is closed.
Canada's flour exports have been dropping consistently for the last 20 years, in spite of an increase in world demand for flour. That increase in world demand is up by over 50 per cent. In 1954 Canadian millers were exporting about 20,142,824 cwts. of flour annually. By 1975 these exports were down to about 8,426,370 cwts., and that is considerably more than 50 per cent. During this same interval the number of active Canadian flour mills dropped off from a peak of 78 to the current 31. This dramatic downturn in Canadian flour production and export is due mainly to subsidy policies of foreign governments, especially the United States and the European Economic Community.
With the exception of these "at and east" rates Canada has chosen not to give further assistance to our flour milling industry. In addition, Canadian export flour always has had to contend with higher seaboard costs compared with our chief competitor, the United States.

The repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act represents increased railway rates from $17.64 to $22.05 per metric ton on flour exports, and that, in the opinion of the Canadian National Millers' Association, and I quote, "will virtually guarantee the speedy demise of Canada's already eroded export flour trade", and even more so, that of our western flour mills.
If this proposed action to bring an end to the "at and east" freight rates is an example of the user pay concept of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), then it is most apparent that this action will impose a cruel hardship on a small sector of our total Canadian industry, which is completely unwarranted and very shortsighted.
The 1961 statutory flour rates were established for four principal reasons: first, to encourage the continued use of existing eastern seaports; second, to help keep Canadian flour mills competitive in world markets; third, to complement, promote, and assist in the expansion of Canada's grain industry, especially in western Canada; and fourth, to benefit our entire Canadian economy with obvious spinoff benefits, not the least of which is improving Canada's balance of trade position with regard to our manufactured goods.
Fifteen years later these same reasons are still every bit as valid as they were back in 1961. Surely in its zeal for restraint of government spending this portion of the bill cannot really be considered as such because of the total net effect it will have on loss of production and loss of jobs to our entire economy, and let us not forget the loss of what is left of our export flour markets. That is why I say the policy is short-sighted. Russia has made it clear that in its opinion, even before this bill becomes law, Canada is no longer competitive in world markets. The Russians have also indicated they will look elsewhere for Cuba's flour supply or, as another alternative, will finance their own flour mills in Cuba. In any event, the result for Canada is less export demand for our flour which is produced by an industry that worked at only 76.6 per cent of its capacity in the 1975 crop year. I would think the biggest part of that shortage in capacity is in the flour mills in western Canada.
We should not overlook another aspect of the implications of this freight rate increase. The new higher rates will be commercial tariff rates, not subject to the same government scrutiny as are the existing compensatory rates.
In his contribution to the debate last Friday the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Goodale) said the Minister of Transport would be contributing to the debate later, and indeed we have just heard him. The parliamentary secretary said that the minister would explain to the opposition, and to the industry, the details which have been worked out to provide a more sensible, economic, and effective method of dealing with the problems of th milling industry. It is unfortunate that these remarks were not made at the beginning of the debate, for rather obvious reasons.
The minister has just finished saying that the net effect of these would be perhaps to lower the cost of transportation to
November 10, 1976

the Canadian people. I wonder at what expense. If it means the demise of the flour milling industry in western Canada, and I see this possibility, then it is a short-sighted policy. 1 am sure there are ongoing discussions on this important matter with the Canadian National Millers' Association, and the minister indicated that. 1 hope that when the bill goes before the standing committee the association will be called so that we can hear their evidence on why the Canadian flour industry cannot continue to compete with export subsidies offered by other countries when ours are being eliminated.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I suggest it is appropriate to point out an inconsistency between the probable net result of clause 15, if implemented, and the recent proposal for future action by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) when he announced a $358 million program to stimulate future employment some time next year. Surely clause 15 would have just the opposite effect-that of reducing employment in the flour milling industry and other ancillary activities. I have to come to the conclusion that clause 1 5 should be deleted from the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take much of the time of the House this afternoon, but I was prompted to try to get in a few minutes on the particular subject discussed by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) who just spoke. Before doing so, however, may I make a few general remarks.
I am continually amazed when hon. members opposite from all parties, but particularly the official opposition, speak with great expression of concern about government spending, overspending, waste, spillage, and so on. When we come to deal with that general question, however, as we do in a bill like C-19, they can see nothing right or proper in it. They speak with forked tongues, as the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin) says.
This is a very important bill, Mr. Speaker, and is of concern to all members regardless of their political affiliation. It is important that the tax dollars we spend are well spent. A bill of this kind affords an opportunity to review some of our programs. It is always painful to reduce or delete a government program, whether it is the Company of Young Canadians or any other. There are many good things to be said for the expenditures as well as the criticism of them.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat referred to two subjects that I should like to deal with briefly. One is the fact that through this bill the government's contribution to the Grain Stabilization Fund will be deferred. He was correct when he pointed out that there is absolutely no change in the government's obligation to make payments into that fund. I do not think it is a fair comparison to say, as perhaps farmers can justifiably say, "Why do you not do the same thing with our 2 per cent?" On the one hand we are talking about a government commitment in the legislation to double the total producer contribution into the fund each year and we are asking, in trying to find government revenues and put them to best
Restraint of Government Expenditures use, for the right to defer those payments. There is certainly no question about the government's obligation in this respect.
Perhaps my hon. friend would agree that the time may not be very distant when we might be making payments out of that fund in view of the current price of wheat. I am glad there is a stabilization plan in effect that will help meet that situation, when and if we run into it, as we have in the past. The clouds on the horizon indicate we might be back in that situation sooner than we would like. The government's obligation has not changed in any way, however.
I regret that more than 30,000 western producers have decided to opt out of the plan. I do not put that down to the fact that farmers are not prepared to accept the trust or confidence of this government; however, they have been listening to some of the chatter and nonsense in the discussions that led up to this bill, although I certainly cannot say that of the hon. member for Medicine Hat. Many members of the NDP and provincial NDP governments, however, have belittled the government's effort to shore up the grain farming industry in the west. If a number of farmers are opting out I would say it is due to the kind of negativism that preceded the debate on the grain stabilization bill.
The other point raised by the hon. member for Medicine Hat referred to the "at and east" rates and what is happening to the flour milling industry in eastern Canada, and the downgrading of that industry that has taken place over the years in western Canada. I am sure he is much more familiar with this matter than I, but I have seen mills close in Saskatoon over the last few years and certainly that is a concern of the government as well as of my hon. friend. I do not see how the "at and east" rates could influence that one way or the other, however. It cannot in western Canada. I suspect my hon. friend had his speech written on the subject before he came into the House.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), in response to a question of legitimate concern raised by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) in his remarks, spelled out that a subsidy will be paid to the milling industry to make sure it will not be harmed. Further, I suggest that the present method of subsidy payment which involves several seemingly unnecessary stops in the movement of the grain from western Canada is not a method the hon. member for Medicine Hat would wish to see continued, since it rules out further possibilities. For instance, I am going to Rosetown on Friday to attend, with many others, the opening of a new inland terminal. I know that this subject will raise political arguments with my hon. friends opposite; but it represents a new, innovative approach, and a different way of doing something. We shall try using the new system and are looking at it. Under the "at and east" rates there is no room for that kind of operation to succeed at any point.
I hope the hon. member for Medicine Hat will review the remarks of the Minister of Transport this afternoon, reconsider his own position and agree with me that in deleting that

November 10, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
particular section of the Railway Act we are not harming the milling industry of eastern Canada or western Canada but are attempting to apply the subsidy in a different way, in a manner which will not rule out other methods of operation.
I suggest that members from western Canada on both sides of the House will support a concept providing for the direct shipment of grain to Saint John and Halifax during the winter months. The Canadian Wheat Board and the railways have such a concept in mind. If that kind of grain movement is viable, surely members on both sides of the House want to encourage the Wheat Board and the railways to bring the trains into operation, hopefully before the year is over. Let us try some innovations and try to get a better return for the subsidies we pay in transport. Hopefully we shall be able to do some new things which will bring better and beneficial results to users at the western end of the system, and shippers, and to receivers at the other end, be they domestic consumers or exporters.
I hope hon. members opposite will support the proposals put forward this afternoon. I am sure the hon. member for Halifax will after he reads Hansard, for I am certain the measures we are considering deserve his support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the introduction of Bill C-19 on second reading gives us a chance to discuss specific recommendations the government has brought forward in this omnibus bill, and a chance to criticize government expenditures.
At the outset of my remarks let me say that the subsidy for flour is not well understood, one reason being the change in the rules whereby consideration of estimates was taken out of this House. I think this bill could have been discussed with greater accuracy and knowledge if the estimates had been considered in this House. As it is they are considered in committee, and the committee is a government organ. Further, in committee one cannot examine adequately all government spending, and it is impossible for the opposition to pin ministers or officials down in a way which was possible in previous years.
Remember, this bill deals with relatively minuscule amounts of money. This is all the more apparent if one remembers that the three levels of government in this country spend over 50 per cent of our Gross National Product. We hear much talk of emotional issues like bilingualism but forget that federal government spending is responsible for a great deal of the divisiveness apparent in the country at present. Government policies have harmed the financial stance of this country and imposed serious strains on confederation. As I say, much of our divisiveness is the result of Ottawa's attempt to impose a uniform level of health, welfare, and education on this country. There has been an attempt at income redistribution, as is evident if one examines the family allowances program. The government felt that in theory every person should be entitled to the same level of social services across the country. The theory has not worked well and has created stresses and strains in Canadian confederation.
(Mr. McIsaac.J
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who has just returned from Japan, suggests that we need increased trade; he also suggested that after the government had laid the groundwork it was up to business people to take over. Considering that all levels of government take more than 50 per cent of our Gross National Product in taxes, some of which they try to redistribute, and considering that Crown corporations like Air Canada, Canadian National, provincial hydro commissions, Petro-Canada and others all have a big stake in how this country is run, the emphasis the Prime Minister places on what private enterprise can do is amusing.
It has been said that if any government of a country takes through taxes more than 35 per cent of Gross National Product the free market in that country will not function. We see an example in the United Kingdom where the standard of living has been forced down because of the breakdown of the economy. This in turn will lead to lower productivity which will be reflected in a still lower standard of living for all in that country.
If I may turn to family allowances, I note an article in a recent edition of the Financial Post datelined Ottawa which suggests that top people in the Income Tax Department, under the direction of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and the deputy minister, are looking at the federal government's income transfer programs to decide which ones can be removed or transferred to the income tax system. It is hoped that this might curtail the large number of bureaucracies required to administer existing social programs. The idea is that Canadians would become their own bureaucrats, as it were, by virtue of a new set of deductions; and that those earning too little to pay tax would receive a direct payment from the government.
Although the article suggests that all aspects of transfer payments are being considered, it is obvious that the government has narrowed its consideration. For instance, perhaps through the tax system it could provide an oil subsidy for low income people; or money could be provided mainly for family allowances and old age pensions. Perhaps this amendment to the Family Allowances Act is the forerunner of some such provision.
When the white paper on taxation was debated, Ontario suggested tax shelters for poor people but the government of the day was not susceptible to such arguments or did not view them with favour. Theoretically, although such a program might slash several billion dollars from federal government spending, the program would not be without its costs. There might be some saving in reality, but the net costs of the program would still need to be met. The only saving that would come about would be a saving in bureaucracy. What the plan really looks at is whether there would be a form of guaranteed income or tax credit to give the impression that great savings are being made. This runs into problems at the time of elections when governments like to give out goodies in the way of new programs. At the present time the government is under fire for spending too much.
November 10, 1976

I want to detail some of the problems of a negative income tax or a minimum income such as has been proposed. In my town there was a joint dominion-provincial plan whereby the residents were given a minimum income. After careful analysis of families, the two governments paid a supplementary income to those who were employed in order that they might have an acceptable standard of living. This was an interesting experiment, and it certainly had its problems. According to newspaper reports, the federal government cancelled the program. There was also a pilot project in the north end of Winnipeg. Most pilot projects were cancelled after the government spent a reputed $ 17 million, according to press reports.
While there are many unfortunate social events flowing out of a minimum income, as I observed it in my community, it is too bad it was terminated before a final decision could be made and the test project analyzed as to the effects of giving a guaranteed income to a controlled group of people. A scientific assessment could have been made of the project.
It is interesting to observe a minimum income project. In the one which I observed there was a definite upgrading of the standard of living for those on low income. As I understand it, in order to qualify you could not be on welfare, but working a good part of the time. Some people left full time jobs for part time employment. Others, faced with the prospect of losing unemployment insurance benefits and a minimum income reduced the amount of their part time work in order to continue enjoying the benefits. Labour was somewhat scarce for unattractive jobs such as pick and shovel jobs, or other jobs people did not want because they were dirty, messy, or at the low end of the work schedule. It allowed people to have a higher standard of living without increasing their production or income.
One of the obvious problems in a rural area in particular was how to deal with the self employed. It seemed difficult. As I understood the official report, it was difficult to assess the income of self employed people. Money could be earned through the sale of produce. Income could be gained by making sales in the names of other members of the family and not reporting this. An enormous amount of administration was required. It is unfortunate that the program was terminated before the scientific results could be ascertained.
The financial outlook for this country, and indeed for the western world, is serious. This was voiced by Mr. Arthur Smith when speaking in Winnipeg last week. He suggested there is more than an even chance for a severe economic slump. The present upturn is weak and we could well slide back to an economic depression. He suggested that Canada would suffer more than most other countries because it is in a generally very weak domestic and international economic position.
Conflicting views of the economic outlook are causing growing uncertainties amongst consumers, businessmen, and government officials. Further, gloom is spreading in the business and financial centres of Europe over the prospect of the world economy to tackle the problems of debt management, sluggish
Restraint of Government Expenditures growth, and rising unemployment. Britain and Italy with their problems are little worse off than a whole series of industrialized countries such as France, Denmark, Ireland, Belgium, Australia and New Zealand.
The poor nations of the developing world are in even worse shape with a mountain of $135 billion in debts and no one can see how this can be paid back. It has been suggested that if the debts to the private banks are not forgiven, there could well be a collapse.
I wish to speak for a moment about grain stabilization. This bill seeks a delay on putting money into the fund. It has been stated that 30,000 wheat board permit holders have opted out of the plan. This is because it has not been on a person-to-person basis. It can be said that any farmer likely to retire within five to ten years has little to gain by staying in the plan. That may be wrong, but I say to the parliamentary secretary that this concern has been voiced to me many times. The plan is seen as an over-all plan for communities and the economy at large.
If a farmer is not in a wheat growing area, and if wheat is not the main grain which he is growing, he is faced with the problem of payment for his grains, primarily barley, wheat and flax, which may be quite remunerative, being made on the basis of how the industry fares with regard to how much it grows and what it sells for, if it does sell.
If the plan had been for the individual, and I see no reason why it could not have been, many more people would have been willing to accept it. For those nearing the end of their farming career, the plan provides little way of getting their money out when they retire. This is one of the major difficulties in connection with the plan.
Second, stabilization plans are made in advance on the basis of past experience; when the time comes to use them they are often found to be deficient, circumstances having changed. We find this happening in the case of grain stabilization arrangements. The $25,000 limit applicable to an individual under grain stabilization is not nearly sufficient, and unless it is raised the reaction of many farmers will be less than favourable.
I should like to mention now a development in the selling of grain which is causing considerable comment in the farm community. The grain stabilization program is, of course, vitally concerned. The Wheat Board, in its assessment of selling prospects for the coming year, concluded that the opportunities available to us were pretty slim. In these circumstances the board made special sales to the private grain trade, there being few government-to-government contracts available-the outlook for sales to the Chinese and to the Russians did not seem very promising; perhaps the Chinese, preoccupied with the changes taking place within their political system, are waiting before they buy. In any case it is reported that forward sales covering 165 million bushels were made to private grain traders at a low price of around $3.75 a bushel. But the private grain trade has hedged. The grain is still in the elevators and

on the farms. The traders are betting that the price of grain will rise.
It is significant that the sales are made by Canada on the exchanges in Chicago and Kansas City, taking advantage of facilities in those places which are not available to the Wheat Board in this country. But it is not possible for dealers to hedge without a cost being incurred. The profit will be made by those who took the hedge. Supposedly the Wheat Board sold on the market to preserve the price. However, the action of the board had the effect of lowering the price of wheat on the Chicago market where prices are largely set.
I notice that Mr. Kristjanson, one of the commissioners, suggested that United States traders were too pessimistic with regard to the price likely to be paid for wheat on world markets in the coming year. But, surely the Wheat Board was pessimistic when it sold almost one third of its normal deliveries on the private market, an action which appears to contribute a significant departure from normal Wheat Board practice. The course followed by the Wheat Board is one of great interest. It means that the board is using directly, or more likely indirectly, the facilities of the Chicago and Kansas City grain exchanges. For those who are interested in orderly marketing this process seems to be at odds with the stated aims of the board. I am looking forward to hearing an explanation from the minister in charge of the Wheat Board.
Speaking of the flour subsidy I will say only that the events surrounding it are an illustration of what happens when we try to upgrade resources. According to what some people tell us, the best thing for Canada would be to export our flour in the form of baked goods and sliced bread. But we cannot do that, as we have now found out. We have gradually lost our markets for flour over the years because one of the first things countries do when they become industrialized is set up flour mills and grind their own grain. Some economists, as I have just mentioned, assert that we should export only products which have been upgraded. The lesson with respect to flour is a timely one. I followed with interest what the minister had to say on this subject and, for my own part, I hope we can keep our flour exports at a satisfactory level because, during periods of slow wheat sales, income from sales of flour has been of great benefit to western farmers.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before us outlines various changes to implement the government's restraint program announced some time ago. I want to speak about a number of those changes, two in particular. I want to call attention to what I consider to be a blatant lack of leadership by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in ensuring restraint in this country and also to another one of his policies, namely, the subsidy referred to by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie), the "at and east" rates.
We have heard a great deal about restraint in the last few years. There was the anti-inflation program brought down by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his now famous Thanksgiving evening address. There are now to be changes in a whole series of programs, the stopping of indexation in family allowances, the elimination of Information Canada, cuts in the

LIP program, the OFY program and the like. We also have a minister of transportation-

I do not think the minister had to spend so much money in flying around the country.
