speechtext:
I would like to ask whether any member in this House can justify the Minister of Transport on any other minister going by Jetstar from here to Montreal and return. If any member can justify that, I invite him to rise and speak now. The Minister of Transport has done that time and time again. You could almost run to Montreal, and the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) could do so in a couple of hours, or you could travel by bus in two hours, and certainly you could run in two or three hours.
Here is this guy who talks about restraint and who says to my farmers that the Crowsnest rates will probably have to go, and who tells them that the user should pay the total cost of transportation, setting the most extravagant example of any minister. I say to hon. members that Jimmy Carter, the president-elect of the U.S., had the chance to take a government aircraft to his vacation spot a few weeks ago, but he said that was not proper and he was going to pay his own way when on vacation because he was not going on official government business. If that is the practice in the United States, why cannot the ministers in this government set that type of example to our people? It is beyond me why they cannot.
Perhaps I could make one more point on that subject. Some of the trips that the Minister of Transport has made are not, in my humble opinion, on government business. Last weekend he addressed a meeting of young Liberals in Saskatchewan. I understand that that type of thing has happened in the past. When he addresses a partisan political meeting of either young or old Liberals, that proportion of the flight should be paid by the minister or by the Liberal Party of Canada. If he has four meetings and one is with Liberals, the party should pay for one quarter of the cost. That would be fair.
The other point I wanted to make is that under this bill there will be a repeal of "at and east" rates. This is the rate that deals with shipment by rail of grain and flour from the Georgian Bay elevators and other elevators in Ontario to the city of Halifax and the city of Saint John in New Brunswick. The movement involves about 30 million bushels of western grain per year at a cost, in the form of a subsidy, of about $11 million to the federal government. This works out to a subsidy of about 33 cents per bushel of wheat.

There are many effects this may have on both the prairie economy and the economy in the Atlantic provinces. First of all, the Canadian Wheat Board, because of the lack of a subsidy, may halt all rail shipments from inland ports to Atlantic ports during the winter months, and they will do it because of the straight economics of moving that grain.
Second, a loss of business and employment in the elevators in Halifax and Saint John will result. We all know that the Atlantic provinces have a high rate of unemployment. The Halifax elevator is owned by the government, but CPR which owns the Saint John elevator is expected to close it down.
Finally, elevators at Georgian Bay will be put out of business since the storage and forwarding of western grain is their major source of income. It will also create additional difficulties for the Canadian Wheat Board in meeting export targets.
While the federal government people say that the Canadian Wheat Board will off-set the discontinuation of shipments in the winter months through Atlantic ports by increased shipments through Vancouver, it is obvious that in years of high volume exports the west coast ports area is already strained to capacity. Second, it does not seem reasonable to ship western grains destined for Europe through Vancouver. It would seem therefore that from now on shipments of grain to Europe will be interrupted for three months or more each year.
For reasons such as these, reasons which I think will cause difficulties to the prairie farmers and the prairie economy, and which will cause unemployment in areas where these elevators are located, particularly in Halifax and Saint John, I hope the government will reconsider the provision in the bill which deals with "at and east" rates.
In conclusion I want to say that a number of other members in my caucus have talked about other aspects of the bill before me, or will be doing so in the days to come. But I want to say that if the government seriously expects the Canadian people to support the anti-inflation program, it must start showing leadership in the House. The Minister of Transport himself must start acting like an adult, not like a little child with a toy. He has to show some leadership in the House. If that is done, then perhaps more Canadians will have confidence in the government and will not be as cynical about the political system that we have in our country. It is the type of example set by the Minister of Transport that makes people really cynical about the federal government and federal institutions. This country is too important to me and to all of us in the House for us to allow it to fall apart for reasons such as I have stated today, for lack of leadership and lack of a good example.
There are many other things that could be referred to and about which other hon. members in my party will be talking. One of them is the unemployment rate which is very high. This means that there should be more stimulation in the economy and that the government should show leadership in that direction, which it is not doing.
My time is running out, Mr. Speaker, so I will take my seat and listen to the speeches of other hon. members in the hope

that the Minister of Transport will perhaps rise and apologize to the House for his conduct, and perhaps one of the members opposite will take up my challenge and speak up on whether or not he thinks the minister should be using a private government jet to fly from here to Montreal and back.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to enter this debate to support this bill which seeks authority for the government in specific ways to restrain its own expenditure program and to reduce it in certain items. I do not propose to debate the relative merits of this or that item which is being restrained, nor the over-all size of the restraint program so far as it is expressed in government expenditures.
There is no doubt that the restraint and reductions by this government are important elements in the battle against inflation and in giving the private sector confidence that the total program is going to work, because government expenditures are one of the main elements that have to be brought under control in order to rebuild that confidence.
There is no doubt that the restraint in government spending is taking hold and 1 would like to give the House some evidence of that. First, there is the $1.5 billion of expenditures less than had been planned. Second, there is the holding of hirings in the federal civil service to levels well below the growth of total employment in our economy, levels of 1.5 per cent increase in this fiscal year and 1 per cent increase in the next fiscal year. These are evidences of a serious intent to reduce the size of the claims of this government on the economy.
Again, the total expenditures of this government in the current fiscal year are estimated to grow by 13 per cent. That is at the same rate as the general economy. That is a significant reduction over previous recent periods, and the total expenditures in our next fiscal period are scheduled to grow at an 11 per cent increase. That also will be at or, indeed, below the increase in the general economy. I cite these as evidences of the serious intent to get the government's share of the economy under control and to hold it under control.
The main points I want to make this evening are that these measures will not be sufficient in themselves to rebuild longterm confidence that the total size of the public sector, as reflected in government spending, will, over the long term, be contained and grow at no greater rates than the economy. To put it another way, confidence requires that the size of the government's claim on the economy will be of no greater proportion than the increase in the total economy; that is, it will have to come out of increased productivity. Why is there not that confidence today? If I can give a few figures, I think it will be somewhat clearer. What is the record of the past ten years? I want to cite only a few figures.
If we go back ten years to fiscal year 1965-66 we find that the total outlays of the federal government were $9.4 billion. Seven years later, in fiscal year 1972-73, they were $20 billion, and three years later, in the fiscal year just ended, they were
Restraint of Government Expenditures $37.3 billion. In the fiscal year in which we now find ourselves they are expected to be over $42 billion. There is here a 10-year growth from $9.4 billion to $42 billion.
How do we cope with these kinds of magnitudes? Let us relate these figures to the total economy. Let us consider the government's expenditures as a percentage of the gross national economy. Ten years ago, in the years I have quoted, the federal government was spending 17 per cent of total expenditures. That rose to 19.1 per cent three years ago and to 23.1 per cent in the previous fiscal year. Through this restraint program it is stabilizing at 23 per cent. However, over the 10-year period the proportion of the Gross National Product spent or taken by this government rose from 17 per cent to 23 per cent. That in itself is one of the factors behind the unwillingness to have confidence in the government, even though it has entered, in a short-term sense, into a restraint program.
The actual increases I have mentioned are readily accounted for. They do not come about just by slippage or lack of efficiency; they do not come about by lack of design; they are the result of deliberate policy choices that we in parliament made and which we on this side of the House supported. So the question is not simply one of not being able to manage. It is a question of deliberately letting the state, for certain policy reasons, take a larger share of the economy.
What were the basic elements in the increase? In the seven years from 1965 to 1972 the government's share grew by 2 percentage points of the national economy. That increase can be accounted for totally by the following three programs: hospitals and medicare, which grew by 0.9 per cent of the economy; old age security and guaranteed income supplement, where we did make the choice that we should increase pensions and index them to the cost of living, and that accounts for 0.7 percentage points of the 2.1 per cent increase; and the third major factor is the equalization payments to the provinces which increased by 0.5 per cent of the total 2.1 per cent increase.
Hospitals and medicare, pensions, and equalization payments to the provinces, which in turn go to the people, are the three programs which account for the growing size of this government's expenditures in that 7-year period. All those increases were payments to people, and not many of us would say that we should not have made them.
In the next three years, the three years which come down to the year which has just ended as a fiscal year, the growth in government spending was four percentage points, a much greater rate of increase than the 2.1 per cent increase in the previous seven years. The major share of this increase was taken by programs which are readily accountable for. We all know how oil transfer payments worked. The export tax on exports to the United States was levied. It flowed through this government's treasury and was paid out to equalize the price of imported oil into the eastern part of Canada, but it reflects a rate of increase in our expenditures. Family allowances accounted for another half of one per cent, and we know that those family allowances trebled in the 10-year period from

Revenue guarantees to the provinces account for another major share of the increase, and the unemployment insurance program accounts for 0.5 percentage points of the total of four percentage points. I wanted to say these things because the matters I want to put before the House now are not related to the temporary or passing phases of stabilization effected by moving government expenditures up and down but are related more to the longer term assurances-and ways of giving credibility to those assurances-that this thing is not going to keep growing and growing and growing as a bigger part of the economy without cease, the assurances that even if we are now restraining, the general movement is not going to reassert itself. 1 want to mention three or four ways in which I think we could usefully address ourselves to that problem.
First, I will remind hon. members, if they will allow me, that on October 14 in this House I argued that we in parliament do not effectively control the growth of government spending.

speechtext: Right on, Martin.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
We should not delude ourselves that in those standing committees where we consider estimates we are really controlling government spending. I have made proposals, and I know there is support on the other side of the House. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) has made some very interesting proposals with regard to how we might do a better job in this House. I remind the House that I suggested a 5-year expenditure forecast, that is, looking ahead, and a related five years review of the past so we can have an overview of what is happening over a 10-year stretch. Then we can consider whether we think it is moving ahead too quickly. I suggest a single committee to carry out surveillance over government spending rather than fragmenting our view of it in the 20 or more standing committees that now consider it. I will not dwell any longer on that role which I think parliament itself should be performing better.
Let me turn now to collective bargaining. The general advice that has been given to government by economists over the past generation, stemming from the economic theories of Lord Keynes, has been that government can act as the balance wheel in the economy; that it can move its expenditures up, then move them down, and by so doing can level out the fluctuations in the economy that have pervasive social and economic results. That theory has grave limitations. It is relatively easy to increase spending but very difficult to decrease it. There comes to exist a built-in growth factor and the level of increase continues. There is a built-in bias.
I think Lord Keynes and we ourselves neglect the role that collective bargaining, as we practise it, plays in leading the economy into inflation and therefore requiring this kind of reactive and unstable government activity which I think is wrong. It is as if the adversary system of collective bargaining operates outside the economy; as if it takes place on the margins and from time to time gets out of hand.
I want to consider one aspect of collective bargaining that is under our control, and that is public service collective bargaining. Seven or eight years ago we imported into public service bargaining the adversary conflict system that is practised in the private sector. I do not think that system belongs in public service bargaining. One reason is that the government is not an employer like any other. Governments cannot be put out of business. If they are pressed for higher salaries or better conditions and grant them they are not going out of business because they simply turn to the tax system to regain the revenues. They are not in the market where there are constraints that bring discipline to bear on collective bargaining, as is the case in the private sector. The services supplied are often monopoly or essential services and, when disrupted, there is grave injury to the third party, the public, in a sense that does not apply to the private sector.
The rate of increase in public service collective bargaining settlements has been such that recently they have been leading the private sector bargaining to ever higher levels. We must find some way of containing those elements in the inflationary spiral and not rely exclusively on fiscal and monetary techniques or raising and lowering government expenditures.
I should like to propose that we consider an alternative system to the adversary system; a system known as fair comparison with jointly selective outside analogues-that is, employees working in comparable employment in the private sector. I will not describe this in detail, but the principle is socially just and more economically sound than the adversary system now practised which we deliberately brought into the public service. Under the fair comparison principle, public service unions and the government jointly would agree that the compensation for public employees is not what they fight each other for or the maximum they can get, but they agree that what they are seeking is a fair comparison with what employees with similar responsibilities are getting from good employers in the private sector. A pay research bureau would make the comparison.
The system is socially just because our employees would be receiving what good employers are paying, no more and no less. If we pay them more-and we are likely to do that at present because we are not restrained by the market and when there is a disruption in service we are under very severe political pressure to concede-if we pay them more we are in effect taxing employees in comparable positions in the private sector. That means the public sector would lead the private sector to higher and higher levels of compensation, with adverse implications for our international competitive situation. I think I need say no more about the difficulties involved.

November 10, 1976

All I want to suggest as an anti-inflation measure which is socially just and economically sound, is that we move to fair comparison as a basis for collective bargaining in the public service.
Then what about the private sector? 1 do not want to talk about collective bargaining in the private sector in the same way, but I want to suggest that we will be intermittently in and out of controls and in and out of government expenditures if we do not use this year of the controls program to build the consultative institutions that will help us with consensus policies for the future and therefore prevent future blowouts in the economy.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) made some suggestions about consultative institutions and I think his are the very minimal proposals. 1 do not know if they have enough structure in the institutional sense to give credibility to the consultative process which he is proposing. I am going to take a few minutes to suggest that we need consultative mechanisms with more institutional structure to them than the minister has suggested, but since my time is expiring 1 shall just run through them rapidly.
What we require is social and economic consultative council in which business, labour, consumers, agriculture, the scientific and other communities are included, but not the government because the government is going to consult that body. These are the main elements in the economy that should be brought face to face with the facts. But where do they get those facts? Before going on to that, Mr. Speaker, I should say that by law the government should be required to consult such a body and to lay before us in this House the results of that consultation. All these lines should lead back to parliament and not just represent some powerful, organized bodies that are carving up the pie, so to speak.
I suggest that we amend or change the structure and role of the Economic Council of Canada; that in future it be an agency of forecasting and of analysis of the economy; that it include government representation and, by invitation, include provincial government appointees. Looking at the economy as it is performing, considering the policies that are in place, and looking at the potential of the economy, this body would provide data and advice to the consultative council but not necessarily to the government. The Economic Council of Canada now advises government and 1 am suggesting that we alter its position, increase its role, and make it an adviser to the consultative council by providing it with the basic data. It would become a workshop and provide data at which all parties could look.
Third, to return to my basic theme, the public sector is not sufficiently co-ordinated to play its role in a consultative process. Similarly we, in parliament, are not equipped to control government spending; nor are governments able jointly to play their role effectively in the Canadian economy. I say that because of this. We, in this parliament, could adopt one course, the provinces could adopt a contrary course, and each
Restraint of Government Expenditures side could frustrate the programs and policies of the other. Meetings of finance ministers are not enough; the ad hoc meetings of other ministers are not enough. Therefore if we are to make the consultative process credible and enter into dialogue with business, labour, consumers and others, we need to obtain a consensus and then undertake commitments.
Mr. Speaker, we in the public sector are not in a position to fulfil our commitments because we do not have all the levers of government at our disposal. Some of them are dispersed among our provinces. I therefore propose the setting up of a federal-provincial stabilization and growth committee whose members would be senior economic ministers. They would consult among themselves, be the main elements representing government in its dealings with the consultative council, undertake commitments, and seek to co-ordinate the responses of the public sector with those commitments made in the consultative process. Only if we establish some such structure will consultation bring substantive effects.
Hon. members may ask, why consultation? 1 suggest that unless we adopt that kind of approach we shall see collective bargaining driving the economy in various directions, with prices mainly going up; we shall see the government over-utilizing fiscal and monetary policies to cope with that situation; and we shall see government expenditures moving upward and downward. We know that if the economy sags we push expenditures up for economic and social reasons. Once expenditures have risen it is hard to bring them back down. That game is becoming obsolete. If we are to correct it we must adopt the refinement and stabilizing effect of a credible consultative process. At present, any such proposed processes lack structure. I am merely suggesting a few ways in which we can be helpful.
Let me add that I am not discussing tripartism. I am discussing only consultative and not decision-making arrangements. I suggest, however, that there is a place for tripartism in the administration of some of our programs and agencies. For example, the Unemployment Insurance Commission might well be administered by government, business and labour; the same applies to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I could name other programs and agencies with respect to which this could be done.
The question is, why do it? By participating in the implementation of such programs all parties concerned would come to have confidence in themselves. After all, they would be administering that which parliament has already enacted and with respect to which guidelines exist. They would not be making fundamental decisions. By working together the parties would come to know each other and understand the need for restraint.
Again, I suggest that the proposal of the Minister of Labour for more collaboration in the work place is sound. I refer to such things as works councils, co-determination, the making of decisions jointly by labour and management, and sharing in managements' decisions at certain levels. Why is all this important? It would involve the grass roots, where the parties can enter into relationships other than adversary relationships.

November 10, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures At the grass roots all the parties concerned may collaborate for greater productivity. That is where the labour side of the equation takes an interest in the success of an enterprise and where the management side gains some understanding of the concerns of labour. As 1 say, this would happen at the grass roots level where both sides would learn to place confidence in the consultative process and allow central bodies representing them in the major consultative council to negotiate on their behalf.
I am suggesting ways in which consultative institutions and mechanisms could be developed, to give future economic activity greater stability and help to avoid the kinds of destabilizing activities in which we are currently engaged.
My final point is this. The public sector has grown to its present size because in some cases the private sector has not been able to perform certain functions. The greatest challenge we face is giving scope, stability, confidence, and strength to the private sector. Only if that sector grows, prospers, provides jobs and incomes, will we be able to restrain the growth in the public sector. Therefore our policies must encourage productivity. Consultative institutions are the best path we know to increased productivity. They mitigate adversary relationships. They arouse interest in both parties in productivity; they are our means of escaping from an ever-growing public sector.
We cannot afford the notion of slow growth in Canada. Slow growth will mean increasing public sector involvement, something we must face. We need high, sustainable growth if we are to restrain our own roles. We should reject slow growth. I would only add that we are on the wrong tack-1 was going to say pursuing the wrong trade policies, but I will not put it so bluntly. We will need to reexamine our economic policies and focus attention on the private sector, because only if the private sector prospers will we restrain our own role.
In my view the greatest source of economic growth in Canada lies in the west. I am not unsympathetic to those across the aisle who complain about specific items in this restraint program. To me they reflect a basic difficulty in the government's perception of economic opportunities in western Canada. In the processing of commodities for example we see value added. There is an interface between transport and processing. For instance, why do we ship oil seeds to Japan? We shipped 15 million bushels and the Japanese processed the oil seeds and made end products. Are we subsidizing Japanese employment? We ship seed to Japan because it is cheaper to send seed than to send the oil. And in this regard one can discern the interface between raw materials, processing and transportation.
Transportation is the key to unlocking economic development in the west and raising "value added." The same may be said for livestock which is turned into meat, grain which becomes flour, and other commodities. We can consider an entire range of economic policies which would be good for Ontario and good for all Canada. Such policies would increase the size of our internal market and trade between our regions and so fulfil the aims of policies designed 100 years ago when our transportation system was established.
* (1750)
However, the destiny that was allowed to western Canada was a resource destiny. That is passe. All the frustration in the west is not psychological. The frustration is transportation and certain trade and tariff policies which do not permit the western economy to rise from the resource destiny to the secondary manufacturing and technological industries that are available today. That is where the private sector could find its greatest expansion. That is where our economic policies should be focused.
I conclude as I began by saying that the temporary measures that came about for stabilization reasons will not rebuild confidence in the long term that the public sector is being restrained. We need longer term measures. I have suggested a few.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext: It has to do with a debate he and I have had for some time. In his desire for greater growth does he foresee great difficulties because of energy shortages and the cost of energy, making necessary a different kind of growth, a slower growth?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a good question. The answer is not all that difficult. I am suggesting that we can have high sustained growth by shipping less oil and more petrochemicals. That would not use up our energy resources any faster than at the present time. In fact it may be a slower use.
What we need is the highest values. That is where the growth is. I am suggesting, for example, the growth would come out of processing oil seeds. A bushel of rapeseed is worth $5 shipped out as rapeseed. It is probably worth $30 shipped out as oil. That is growth, from $5 to $30. What have we expended in energy? Some, yes, but we have gained a lot in terms of income and we can redistribute some of that income.
At the rate we are going, we hear people say let us accept slower growth. I agree you have to protect the environment. To do so contributes to growth. That is an industry in itself. It will come back to us in revenue if we do it. We have to respect the ecology and conserve resources. I say we move them to higher values. That is all I am saying. That is growth. The Gross National Product would rise very rapidly if instead of $5 being added by a bushel, $30 were added by oil. That is growth. That is what we are looking for.
